title: Neural Audio Codecs — EnCodec, SNAC, Mimi, DAC and the Semantic-Acoustic Split

questions.question: Why does an audio language model need a codec before an LLM can predict speech?
options: The codec converts each word directly into a speaker label
The codec removes language structure from the audio signal
The codec expands every sample into a mel frequency bin
The codec turns a continuous waveform into discrete tokens
questions.explanation: A waveform is continuous-valued, but an LLM predicts discrete symbols; a neural codec encodes audio into discrete tokens and can decode them back. A speaker label omits the time-varying audio content and is not the codec token sequence.

questions.question: In residual vector quantization, what does each codebook after the first quantize?
options: The speaker label paired with the current frame
The full output waveform after decoder synthesis
The residual error left by earlier codebooks
A duplicate copy of the original waveform
questions.explanation: The first codebook approximates the encoder output; each later codebook quantizes what remains after the earlier code vectors are subtracted. Repeating the original does not refine the current residual; the decoder instead sums successive residual approximations.

questions.question: At 12.5 frames per second with 8 codebooks, how many tokens represent 10 seconds?
options: 10,000 tokens
1,000 tokens
800 tokens
125 tokens
questions.explanation: Ten seconds × 12.5 frames/second = 125 frames; with 8 codebooks per frame, 125 × 8 = 1,000 tokens. The 125-token option counts one token per frame and omits the eight codebook tokens emitted at each frame.

questions.question: In the lesson’s Mimi split, what does codebook 0 primarily represent?
options: Semantic content such as phonemes and words
Acoustic details such as timbre and background noise
The exact speaker enrollment threshold for verification
The waveform sampling rate and channel count
questions.explanation: Mimi codebook 0 is WavLM-distilled to represent phonetic and linguistic content; codebooks 1–7 encode acoustic residual details. Those details belong to the residual codebooks, not the semantic first codebook.

questions.question: A team is building a streaming speech generator and wants short token sequences with semantic content. Which codec fits the lesson?
options: A 50 Hz EnCodec stream with every codebook removed
Opus as a discrete text-generation tokenizer
Mimi with its low-rate semantic-acoustic split
DAC at 44.1 kHz for maximum reconstruction fidelity
questions.explanation: Mimi combines a low 12.5 Hz frame rate with a semantic-acoustic split, keeping streaming speech token sequences short while retaining content and detail. DAC prioritizes high-fidelity reconstruction at a higher frame rate, producing longer sequences than the streaming-oriented Mimi.

questions.question: A codec has excellent waveform reconstruction but weak linguistic structure for an LM. What lesson should guide the evaluation?
options: Replace the tokenizer with a speaker verification embedding
Check semantic structure as well as reconstruction quality
Choose it because waveform similarity guarantees easy generation
Add more acoustic codebooks without checking sequence length
questions.explanation: An LM needs token structure that separates linguistic content from acoustic detail; waveform reconstruction quality alone does not guarantee that structure. A close reconstruction can still entangle content and acoustics, leaving the language model a harder prediction problem.
